assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory turned the strongly correlated electron problem into a tractable, systematically improvable framework: the Hubbard-model Mott transition, correlated metals and, through DFT+DMFT, realistic calculations of actual materials. It is original, conceptually clear and has become a standard method across oxides, heavy fermions and actinides. From my own work with electronic-structure theory I see its impact directly in how spectra and magnetism of correlated solids are computed.
assessment.attribution: The infinite-dimension limit of lattice fermions (Metzner and Vollhardt) and the mapping onto a self-consistent impurity problem (Georges and Kotliar) are the decisive steps. The supplied credit list lacks Walter Metzner, which I note as a fairness issue I cannot fix within this list. Within the supplied names, Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt form a defensible trio, although Vollhardt's role rests on the Metzner-Vollhardt limit.
assessment.maturity: More than three decades of independent use, extensive cross-validation against experiment and exact methods, and wide adoption in materials theory. Recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether a prize for a method and theoretical framework is preferred to one for a discovery.
Metzner's contribution is absent from the supplied credit list and may complicate a fair configuration.
Limits of the local self-energy approximation are known; I rely on memory for the extent of cluster-extension success.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance, and later the giant effect in crystalline MgO barriers, enabled magnetic read heads and magnetic random-access memory. It is a clear, decisive advance in spin-dependent transport whose technological reach is large and which extends the physics recognised for giant magnetoresistance in 2007. The mechanism, spin-polarised tunnelling and coherent symmetry filtering, is well understood from first-principles theory.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and, separately, Yuasa and colleagues demonstrated the giant MgO effect in 2004. Butler and Mathon predicted the MgO effect theoretically. The supplied trio is credible but the MgO stage may need Yuasa or Djayaprawira, who are not on the list, and Butler's theory is also absent.
assessment.maturity: Technology deployed for roughly two decades in hard drives and MRAM, with robust confirmation. Mature and well timed.
uncertainties: Credit is split between the 1995 discovery and the 2004 MgO stage, and names for the second stage are missing from the supplied list.
Overlap with the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize might be judged too close by some members.
My recollection of the precise priority dates is not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator revealed a new class of band insulator with protected edge and surface states. It is original, conceptually clear and linked to spin-orbit physics that is accessible to first-principles calculations of real compounds. The impact on materials discovery and quantum matter has been broad.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposal; Molenkamp's group carried out the HgTe quantum-well experiment predicted by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. The supplied trio is a reasonable configuration, but Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, as well as Fu, Kane and Mele on the three-dimensional case, are omitted from the credit list.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and in three-dimensional materials by photoemission. The 2016 prize on topological phase transitions covers related ground, so some reviewers may consider the field already honoured.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases.
Competing claims by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not represented in the supplied credit.
Quantum anomalous Hall experiments are a related but separate achievement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in twisted bilayer graphene opened moire materials as a tunable platform for correlated physics. It is a striking combination of theory and experiment and its influence on the field has been large.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction; Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators measured the correlated and superconducting phases in 2018. The supplied trio matches this prediction-plus-experiment structure well. Contributions by the Cao and Fatemi co-authors, and by Dean and others on moire hBN, are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced across many groups, but the interpretation of the correlated and superconducting phases is still being debated. This is at the edge of what I consider mature.
uncertainties: The origin of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states remain contested.
Only about eight years since the experiments, which may be premature.
Student and postdoctoral contributions are not credited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, including the Mott insulator transition, and created a programmable quantum simulator for strongly correlated matter. This has strong conceptual clarity and ties directly to the models I know from correlated electron theory.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch observed the superfluid-Mott transition, and Bloch led much of the later development. The credited trio is coherent, but Jaksch, Hänsch and Esslinger have comparable claims to the original work.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature and widely replicated, though quantum simulation of the harder fermionic problems is still in progress and its payoff relative to classical methods is not settled.
uncertainties: Credit for the early Mott-insulator work involves Greiner, Mandel, Esslinger, Hänsch and Bloch, and the supplied list does not resolve the allocation.
Whether quantum advantage for correlated materials has been demonstrated is uncertain.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity at 26 K in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx opened a second family of high-temperature superconductors, with transition temperatures above 50 K. It overturned the assumption that copper oxides were uniquely suited to high Tc and provides a large testbed for magnetism-superconductivity coupling, which I find directly relevant to magnetic materials theory.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group made the original discovery in 2008 and is a clear candidate for sole credit. Later enhancements of Tc by Chinese groups were important but followed the discovery. Only one name is supplied, so no further decision is possible.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed experimentally across numerous related compounds, though the pairing mechanism is still not settled. Timeliness is reasonable and similar to that of earlier superconductivity prizes that honoured the discovery before the mechanism was known.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism is unresolved.
A prize for a single person leaves out the broader community effort on iron pnictide and chalcogenide development.
The lower maximum Tc and limited applications reduce the practical impact compared with the cuprates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultrasoft pseudopotentials and the projector augmented-wave method made large-scale first-principles calculations accurate and efficient, and they underlie codes such as VASP that are used in a very large fraction of materials calculations. My own field relies on these methods, so I can attest to their significance, but I also acknowledge that I am not a neutral evaluator here.
assessment.attribution: Vanderbilt introduced ultrasoft pseudopotentials, Blöchl formulated PAW, and Kresse and Joubert connected it to a plane-wave implementation; Kresse also led VASP. The supplied trio is a defensible but contestable configuration since Joubert and the broader community contributions are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Used for decades and validated, including in multi-code reproducibility studies. Recognition of computational methods has precedent through the 1998 chemistry prize, but physics-prize fit for method development is less obvious.
uncertainties: Whether the physics prize should recognise computational methods of this type.
Possible conflict of interest because of my own use and expertise.
Allocation between methods theory and software implementation is ambiguous.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The experimental demonstration of intrinsic ferromagnetism in atomically thin CrI3 and Cr2Ge2Te6 showed that long-range magnetic order can persist down to monolayers, contrary to the Mermin-Wagner expectation without anisotropy. This is a clear conceptual advance and it matters for magnetism in reduced dimensions, my own area.
assessment.attribution: The 2017 papers by Xu and collaborators on CrI3 and by Zhang and collaborators on Cr2Ge2Te6 are the decisive experiments. Jarillo-Herrero's role in the CrI3 spin-filter and tunnelling work is relevant but less central to the discovery itself, so the supplied trio contains a likely mismatch with the underlying credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and the fundamentals are secure, but applications are still developing and the work is recent. Recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: Whether Jarillo-Herrero's contributions are decisive for the discovery of intrinsic 2D magnetism.
The field is young and the long-term significance is unclear.
Related claims by Gong, Wang and others are not in the supplied credit.
